market_context: United States; honey and granulated table sugar used as sweeteners
title: Honey vs. sugar: nutrition differences

seo.title: Honey vs. sugar: calories, sugars and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Honey is not simply liquid table sugar. Compare calories, sugar types, tablespoon portions and micronutrients to see what really changes.
seo.search_intent: Compare honey with granulated table sugar nutritionally and understand whether replacing one with the other makes a meaningful difference.

excerpt: Honey contains water plus fructose, glucose and smaller amounts of other sugars; table sugar is almost entirely sucrose. Per 100 g, honey has about 304 calories and 82 g of sugars versus roughly 387 calories and 100 g for sugar, but a tablespoon of honey weighs more: about 64 calories versus about 49 calories in a tablespoon of granulated sugar. Amount used matters more than the small nutritional differences.
content_html:
Swapping a spoonful of white sugar for honey can feel like an obvious nutritional upgrade. Honey has aroma, color, and plant compounds from nectar; granulated sugar looks much simpler. The actual difference is more modest. Honey is not pure sugar, but most of its solids are still sugars.

The useful question is less about declaring one sweetener “healthy” and more about how much ends up in the coffee, yogurt, oatmeal, or recipe.

By weight, honey has fewer calories and less sugar

Honey is roughly 17% water. That water lowers its energy concentration: USDA reference data put honey at about 304 calories and 82 g of sugars per 100 g, while granulated table sugar provides about 387 calories and essentially 100 g of carbohydrate, almost all sugar, per 100 g.

Per 100 gHoneyGranulated sugar
Energy≈304 kcal≈387 kcal
Sugars≈82 g≈100 g
Water≈17 g≈0 g

That is a fair gram-for-gram comparison, but it does not mean a tablespoon of honey contains fewer calories. Volume tells a different story.

A tablespoon reverses the calorie comparison

A tablespoon of honey weighs about 21 g and supplies roughly 64 calories and 17 g of sugars. A tablespoon of granulated sugar weighs around 12.5 g and supplies about 49 calories and 12.5 g of sugar. Honey is less calorie-dense by weight, yet much more mass fits into the same spoon.

So a one-for-one tablespoon swap does not automatically reduce either calories or sugar. If a strongly flavored honey lets you enjoy 10 g instead of 12.5 g of sugar, total intake can fall; if you fill a 21-g tablespoon, it can rise.

The sugar molecules are not arranged the same way

Table sugar is sucrose, a molecule made from glucose and fructose. Honey already contains mostly free simple sugars. USDA analysis places average fructose around 38% and glucose around 30%, with smaller amounts of maltose, sucrose, and other oligosaccharides.

That mixture changes sweetness, moisture, browning, and texture in cooking. It does not make honey's sugars nutritionally invisible. In U.S. labeling, honey used to sweeten a food contributes added sugars, and the Dietary Guidelines recommend keeping added sugars below 10% of daily calories for people age 2 and older.

Honey's micronutrients exist, but the serving is small

Honey contains trace minerals and a range of phenolic compounds that vary with floral source and processing. A 15–20 g serving, however, delivers only small amounts of those nutrients while still supplying roughly 12–16 g of sugars.

That makes honey an inefficient way to chase potassium, iron, or antioxidants. Its aroma, ability to hold moisture, and distinctive flavor are perfectly good culinary reasons to use it; it does not need to function as a multivitamin.

One safety difference is not subtle: infants

Honey should not be given to children under 12 months because it can contain Clostridium botulinum spores associated with infant botulism. Ordinary cooking or commercial pasteurization does not turn honey into an appropriate food for a baby younger than one year.

For older children and adults, that specific restriction does not apply. The everyday question returns to flavor, total added sugar, and the rest of the diet.

If the goal is less sugar, reduce the sweetener

Choose honey when you want honey flavor. If the goal is to cut added sugar, using less total sweetener is more dependable than replacing equal spoonfuls of sugar with honey.

Measured by weight, 10 g of honey provides about 30 calories and 8 g of sugars, versus about 39 calories and 10 g of sugar from 10 g of granulated sugar. That is the real gram-for-gram advantage. A kitchen spoon can erase it because honey is denser.

faq.question: Does honey have fewer calories than sugar?
faq.answer: Per 100 g, yes: about 304 calories versus about 387. But a tablespoon of honey weighs about 21 g and has roughly 64 calories, while a tablespoon of granulated sugar around 12.5 g has about 49 calories.

faq.question: Does honey count as added sugar?
faq.answer: When honey is used to sweeten a food or drink, its sugars count toward added sugars on U.S. labels and in dietary guidance.

faq.question: Can babies eat honey if it has been cooked?
faq.answer: No. Children under 12 months should not be given honey because of infant botulism risk, and ordinary cooking does not remove that recommendation.
